resources.string: ① Show original image

[Principle] No processing is performed; the original image is displayed directly as the reference baseline.\n[Model] Homomorphic filtering of images is based on the illuminance-reflectance imaging model: image f is formed by multiplying the illuminance component i (determined by the light source, varying slowly in space and concentrated at low frequencies) by the reflectance component r (determined by object surface properties, changing sharply and concentrated at high frequencies). The two are intertwined and cannot be separated by linear filtering directly, so they must be processed in the log domain (Eq. 2-81 ~ 2-87 workflow).
② Illuminance component i(x,y) estimation

[Principle] The illuminance component depends on the light source and varies slowly in space (low frequency); the illumination field can be estimated with a large-σ Gaussian low-pass filter (σ=60).\n[Eq. 2-81] f(x,y) = i(x,y)·r(x,y) (image = illuminance × reflectance)\n[Effect] Shows the bright and dark distribution of illumination (slowly varying structures such as shadows and vignetting); an excessive dynamic range results precisely from excessive fluctuation of the illuminance component.
③ Reflectance component r(x,y) estimation

[Principle] The reflectance component depends on object surface properties and changes sharply (edges/details, high frequency). Engineering approximation: r = f / (i + 1), i.e. the original image divided by the illuminance estimate.\n[Eq. 2-81] f(x,y) = i(x,y)·r(x,y)\n[Effect] After normalization, shows the detail and edge structure of objects — this high-frequency reflectance component is exactly what homomorphic filtering enhances.
④ Log domain ln f (Eq. 2-82)

[Principle] Taking the logarithm of the imaging model turns the multiplicative relationship into an additive one, so that the illuminance and reflectance components can be separated linearly in the (log-domain) spectrum.
[Eq. 2-82] z(x,y) = ln f(x,y) = ln i(x,y) + ln r(x,y)
[Eq. 2-83] Z(u,v) = F{z(x,y)} (DFT)
[Eq. 2-84] Z(u,v) = I(u,v) + R(u,v) (illuminance spectrum and reflectance spectrum separated)
[Effect] Shows the normalized image of ln f, an intermediate result before entering frequency-domain filtering.
⑤ Homomorphic filtering, standard parameters (Eq. 2-87)

[Principle] After the DFT in the log domain, filtering is applied with the transfer function H (compressing low-frequency illuminance and enhancing high-frequency reflectance), followed by the IDFT and exponentiation for restoration.
[Eq. 2-85] S(u,v) = H(u,v)·Z(u,v)
[Eq. 2-86] s(x,y) = F⁻¹[S(u,v)]
[Eq. 2-87] g(x,y) = e^s(x,y)
[Transfer function] H(u,v) = (HH − HL)·(1 − e^(−c·D²/D0²)) + HL (Fig. 2-42 profile, Example 2-7)
[Parameters] This demo uses D0=80, c=1.5, HL=0.5, HH=2.0 (classic parameters of Example 2-7, Fig. 2-44)
[Effect] Removes uneven illumination and compresses the dynamic range while enhancing edge details.
⑥ Homomorphic filtering, strong illuminance compression

[Principle] Reduce the low-frequency gain HL (to compress the illuminance component more strongly) and raise the high-frequency gain HH (to enhance reflectance details more strongly).
[Eq. 2-85] S(u,v) = H(u,v)·Z(u,v); [Eq. 2-87] g = e^s
[Transfer function] H(u,v) = (HH − HL)·(1 − e^(−c·D²/D0²)) + HL
[Parameters] This demo uses D0=80, c=1.5, HL=0.2, HH=2.5
[Effect] Dynamic range compression is more obvious and the image is more uniform overall; an excessively small HL causes loss of details in dark areas.
⑦ Homomorphic filtering, cutoff frequency D0=30

[Principle] The cutoff frequency D0 determines the boundary between low and high frequencies: the smaller D0 is, the wider the enhanced high-frequency range becomes, and more mid-frequency components are boosted as reflectance details.
[Eq. 2-85] S(u,v) = H(u,v)·Z(u,v); [Eq. 2-87] g = e^s
[Transfer function] H(u,v) = (HH − HL)·(1 − e^(−c·D²/D0²)) + HL
[Parameters] This demo uses D0=30, c=1.5, HL=0.5, HH=2.0
[Effect] The detail enhancement covers a wide range and textures stand out more, but over-enhancement may occur.
⑧ Homomorphic filtering, cutoff frequency D0=150

[Principle] The larger D0 is, the farther outward the transition of the filter profile lies; only very high frequencies are enhanced, and the processing is dominated by overall dynamic range compression.
[Eq. 2-85] S(u,v) = H(u,v)·Z(u,v); [Eq. 2-87] g = e^s
[Transfer function] H(u,v) = (HH − HL)·(1 − e^(−c·D²/D0²)) + HL
[Parameters] This demo uses D0=150, c=1.5, HL=0.5, HH=2.0
[Effect] Illumination becomes more uniform and the image flatter; detail enhancement is relatively mild.
⑨ Homomorphic filtering, mild enhancement

[Principle] With HL close to 1 and a moderate HH (e.g. 1.5), the filter acts as a gentle high-frequency emphasis and modifies the original image only slightly.
[Eq. 2-85] S(u,v) = H(u,v)·Z(u,v); [Eq. 2-87] g = e^s
[Transfer function] H(u,v) = (HH − HL)·(1 − e^(−c·D²/D0²)) + HL
[Parameters] This demo uses D0=80, c=1.5, HL=0.8, HH=1.5
[Effect] Slightly compresses the illuminance and boosts details, suitable as a conservative homomorphic enhancement scheme.
① Show original image

[Principle] No processing is performed; the original image is displayed directly as the reference baseline.\n[Model] Retinex (retina + cortex) theory holds that the image perceived by the human eye = illumination component × reflectance component (Eq. 2-88), and the color of an object surface depends on its reflectance properties rather than on the illumination. Accordingly, the reflectance component is estimated by subtraction in the log domain, which removes uneven illumination while achieving both dynamic range compression and color constancy (color fidelity) enhancement.
② Illumination component L estimation (Eq. 2-92)

[Principle] The illumination component is estimated by convolving the original image with a Gaussian surround function (center/surround ratio), yielding a slowly varying smooth illumination field.
[Eq. 2-88] f(x,y) = i(x,y)·r(x,y) (Retinex imaging model)
[Eq. 2-92] L(x,y) = I(x,y) * G(x,y) (Gaussian surround convolution)
[Parameters] This demo uses σ=80 (the classic scale of Fig. 2-46)
[Effect] Shows the illumination distribution such as shadows and brightness gradients; uneven illumination is exactly the root cause of the poor quality of dark image regions.
③ Reflectance component r visualization (Eq. 2-90)

[Principle] In the log domain, ln f = ln i + ln r; the logarithm of the illumination is denoted l, so the reflectance component is ln f − l, reflecting the reflective properties of object surfaces.
[Eq. 2-89] ln f(x,y) = ln i(x,y) + ln r(x,y)
[Eq. 2-90] l(x,y) = ln i(x,y), r(x,y) = ln f − l(x,y)
[Parameters] This demo uses σ=80, displayed in grayscale
[Effect] Bright areas stand for strong reflectance (regions rich in details/edges).
④ SSR σ=15 (Eq. 2-91)

[Principle] SSR (single-scale Retinex) applies the logarithmic center/surround ratio operation to each of the R, G, B channels.
[Eq. 2-91] ri(x,y) = ln Ii(x,y) − ln[Ii(x,y)*G(x,y)], i = R,G,B
[Eq. 2-92] G is the Gaussian surround function
[Parameters] This demo uses σ=15 (small scale)
[Effect] Small σ: strong dynamic range compression and prominent details, but with fairly obvious color distortion (Fig. 2-46).
⑤ SSR σ=80 (Fig. 2-46)

[Principle] SSR is single-scale Retinex; the choice of σ is a trade-off between the two kinds of enhancement effects.
[Eq. 2-91] ri(x,y) = ln Ii(x,y) − ln[Ii(x,y)*G(x,y)]
[Eq. 2-92] L(x,y) = I(x,y) * G(x,y)
[Parameters] This demo uses σ=80 (the classic compromise scale, Fig. 2-46)
[Effect] Balances dynamic range compression and color fidelity to a certain extent; the most commonly used single-scale parameter.
⑥ SSR σ=250

[Principle] A large-scale Gaussian surround approaches the global average, so the illumination estimate is very smooth.
[Eq. 2-91] ri(x,y) = ln Ii(x,y) − ln[Ii(x,y)*G(x,y)]
[Parameters] This demo uses σ=250 (large scale)
[Effect] Large σ: high color fidelity and a natural overall look, but insufficient dynamic range compression (Fig. 2-46), with limited brightening of dark areas.
⑦ MSR three-scale (Eq. 2-93)

[Principle] MSR (multi-scale Retinex) takes the weighted average of the SSR results at multiple σ scales, combining the advantages of small scales (details) and large scales (color fidelity).
[Eq. 2-93] R_MSR_i = Σk ωk·{ln Ii − ln[Ii * Gk]}, where k is the scale index
[Eq. 2-94] ωk = 1/N (equal weight for each scale)
[Parameters] This demo uses σ = {15, 80, 250}, N=3
[Effect] Achieves a relatively good balance between detail enhancement and color fidelity; the most commonly used Retinex scheme in engineering.
⑧ MSR five-scale (Eq. 2-94)
⑨ MSRCR color restoration (Eq. 2-96)
① Show original image

[Principle] No processing is performed; the original image is displayed directly as the reference baseline.
[Concept] Color enhancement falls into two categories:
· Pseudo-color enhancement (2.7.1): maps a grayscale image to a color image according to a certain criterion; the number of colors the human eye can distinguish is far greater than the number of gray levels, which improves detail discernibility;
· False-color enhancement (2.7.2): a color-to-color mapping that maps a natural color or multispectral image point by point to a new color space.
② Gray-level slicing, two-level cutting (Fig. 2-47)

[Principle] Place a cutting plane parallel to the xy plane at gray level l1, dividing the image into two regions: pixels below l1 are assigned one color (blue) and pixels above l1 another color (red), yielding a two-color pseudo-color image.
[Fig. 2-47] Cutting schematic of gray-level slicing
[Parameters] This demo uses l1=128 (the median gray level)
[Effect] Segments bright and dark regions in a simple and intuitive way.
③ Gray-level slicing, multi-plane cutting (Fig. 2-48)

[Principle] Use M cutting planes to divide the gray-level range into M+1 regions S1..S(M+1), and manually assign a color to each region, yielding an (M+1)-color pseudo-color image.
[Fig. 2-48] Cutting schematic of multi-level gray slicing
[Parameters] This demo uses M=7 (8 spectral colors evenly distributed in hue)
[Effect] Advantages: simple and easy to implement in software and hardware, and the area of a given gray level can also be counted; disadvantages: the pseudo-colors are stiff and not well harmonized, and the number of colors is limited.
④ Gray-level to color transform (Fig. 2-49)

[Principle] According to the principle of three primary colors, the gray level f is fed into red/green/blue transformers with different transform characteristics; the three primary components IR/IG/IB are output and then combined into color. What is modulated is the pixel gray value rather than the position, producing a continuous color image with multiple color gradients.
[Fig. 2-49] Principle of gray-level to color transformation (typical characteristics of the red/green/blue transformers)
[This implementation] Triangle-wave transformers with phases staggered by 1/3 of a period:
IR = tri(f/255), IG = tri(f/255 + 1/3), IB = tri(f/255 + 2/3), tri(x) = 1 − |2·frac(x) − 1|
[Effect] Gray levels are mapped to a smooth rainbow gradient, with detail layers distinguished by hue.
⑤ Pseudo-color by frequency-domain filtering (Fig. 2-50)

[Principle] Pseudo-color here is unrelated to gray levels but related to spatial frequency content: after the DFT of the grayscale image, low-pass/band-pass/high-pass filters separate the spectrum; each part is transformed back by IDFT, additionally processed (histogram equalization), and displayed as one of the three primary colors.
[Fig. 2-50] Block diagram of pseudo-color enhancement implemented by frequency-domain filtering
[This implementation] R = high-pass (edges → red), G = band-pass, B = low-pass (background → blue); the filters are Gaussian (low-pass D0=30, high-pass D0=60).
[Effect] Edges appear red and slowly varying regions appear bluish, which facilitates the visual detection of boundaries.
⑥ False color, linear mapping (Eq. 2-97)

[Principle] False-color enhancement is a color-to-color mapping that maps a natural color image point by point into a chromaticity space determined by the three primary colors; when redisplayed, the target colors differ from the natural original colors.
[Eq. 2-97] [gR, gG, gB]ᵀ = M·[fR, fG, fB]ᵀ (M is a 3×3 mapping matrix)
[This implementation] Channel-rotation matrix: gR = fB, gG = fR, gB = fG
[Purpose] After the false-color transform, the image is more eye-catching than the original natural colors (purpose 1).
⑦ False color, details to green (Eq. 2-97)

[Principle] According to the physiological characteristics of the human eye, details of interest that are hard to distinguish are assigned colors to which the eye is more sensitive — the human eye is particularly sensitive to green.
[Eq. 2-97] [gR, gG, gB]ᵀ = M·[fR, fG, fB]ᵀ
[This implementation] gG = f (grayscale details as the green channel), gR = gB = low-pass blurred background
[Effect] Targets rich in details appear green-toned and are easier to distinguish (purpose 2).
⑧ False color, details to blue (Eq. 2-97)

[Principle] The human eye has high contrast sensitivity to changes in blue; assigning targets rich in details varying shades of blue can improve the detectability of details.
[Eq. 2-97] [gR, gG, gB]ᵀ = M·[fR, fG, fB]ᵀ
[This implementation] gB = f (grayscale details as the blue channel), gR = gG = low-pass blurred background
[Effect] Details are presented in shades of blue, a demonstration of contrast sensitivity (purposes 2/3).
⑨ False color by multispectral composition (Eq. 2-98)

[Principle] False-color enhancement of multispectral images uses n band images combined into the RGB primaries through the transform functions TR/TG/TB; integrating multiple bands provides more information and makes it easier to distinguish certain features (purpose 3).
[Eq. 2-98] gR = TR[f1..fn], gG = TG[f1..fn], gB = TB[f1..fn]
[This implementation] Treats the RGB channels as three bands f1/f2/f3, with band-difference transform functions:
gR = |f1 − f2|, gG = |f2 − f3|, gB = |f3 − f1|
[Effect] Regions with large spectral differences show vivid colors, highlighting the boundaries of specific materials/targets.
